title: What they said at the time

clips.q: In its rush to develop new products, Coca-Cola Co. within the next 30 days will bring to market a new brand that’s admittedly not fully formed.
It’s the flip side of overclaiming, which is what teens perceive a lot of brands do.
Coke is trying to take it all.
clips.who: **Larry Jabbonsky**, editor of Beverage World, Time, May 30, 1994[^6]

clips.q: I’m much less concerned with how the product tastes and a whole lot more concerned with the fact that it just has sort of major impact.
The first one tastes good, but you don’t want a second.
clips.who: **Darrin Billig**, 20, Minneapolis, The Washington Post, Sep 3, 1994[^8]

clips.q: It’s a game. We’re just playing a more sophisticated game.
clips.who: **Peter Wegner**, Wieden & Kennedy, The Washington Post, Sep 3, 1994[^8]

clips.q: We just didn’t generate the type of profitable volume we needed with OK, so we decided not to continue it in those test markets.
clips.who: **Randy Donaldson**, Coca-Cola, The New York Times, Sep 13, 1995[^9]

clips.q: I knew full well that what they were trying to do was not possible, that you could not market to cynical hipsters by being cynical and hipsterish.
